newsitem.title: USA: PSA sees good and bad news for munis in elections.
newsitem.headline: PSA sees good and bad news for munis in elections.

text.p: Tuesday's presidential and congressional election results are good news and bad news for the municipal bond market, Public Securities Association's executive vice president said.
Micah Green said in a telephone interview that the return of a Republican Congress and a Democrat president means Washington is "staying the course" on general economic policy.
That is good news for a muni bond market that has benefited from deficit reduction, budget balancing efforts and restraints on government spending, Green said.
But Tuesday's results also offer a mixed bag for munis in terms of upcoming congressional legislation, Green said.
"It's safe to say there will be some form of tax bill," Green said.
And while that means opportunities for the municipal market, including legislation to raise congressional caps on the volume of private activity bonds states can issue, it spells risk, Green said.

"With any tax bill that cuts revenue, you have to have revenue raisers to offset (those cuts)," Green said. "Every sector of the economy is at risk and the muni bond market is not short of its risky items," he said.

He said likely to "rear its ugly head" again next year is the Clinton Administration's plan to repeal the two percent "de minimis" rule, which currently makes it easier for corporations to buy municipal bonds.
Also, Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, D-N.Y., probably will reintroduce his controversial bill to end the tax exemption for stadium bonds, Green said.
But Congress could take up another Moynihan proposal backed by muni issuers, Green said.
He referred to Moynihan's recent bill to eliminate the $150 million cap on the amount of tax-exempt bonds that a private non-profit institution, or 501(c)(3) organization, can have outstanding.
Green said tax provisions favorable to munis may be on the horizon as Congress and the Administration move to reauthorize the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act (ISTEA).
And Clinton has a proposal to increase the use of bonds for school construction, Green said.
"Will there be opportunities to deal with (these) muni bond issues? We don't know yet," Green said.
"That's our challenge," he said. "We'll have our work cut out for us."
